119,452 Strava runners. Faster marathoners did more of the ‘slow’ work.

Review your last four weeks: total distance, easy volume and recovery. Build from your own tolerated workload, rather than jumping to a faster group’s average.

#PRPacer #MarathonTraining #RunningResearch #EasyMiles #RunnerTok
altText: 119,452 Strava runners. Faster marathoners did more of the ‘slow’ work.
151,813 marathons. Sixteen weeks of training. The fastest group, finishing in 2:00–2:30, averaged about 107 km/week. The 4:30–5:00 group averaged about 35 km/week.

Most of the extra volume was low intensity. Faster groups accumulated more low-intensity running. The study used three zones, not your watch’s five-zone labels. Absolute time in harder zones was comparatively similar.
Those are groups, not a prescription. The study used 30-minute finish-time groups, not exact sub-2:45 versus sub-4 cohorts. Association cannot prove that copying the mileage causes the same result.

What’s the big deal with bicarb—and why are elites using it?

It is a buffer, not a carb. The appeal is a possible edge when the effort gets very hard. The catch: benefits depend on the event and protocol, and your gut may object.

Continuous-running evidence is mixed: a review found a negligible adjusted average benefit, while a newer small 10K trial reported an improvement. A separate running trial found better gut tolerance with hydrogel but no faster 800 m.

Would you chase the marginal gain—or keep your race-day routine simple?

altText: What’s the big deal with bicarb—and why are elites using it? Photo: Maurten Bicarb System.
Not carbs. Bicarb. Sodium bicarbonate raises the blood’s buffering capacity. That can help manage the hydrogen-ion load associated with very hard exercise. It is not another carbohydrate fuel.

The appeal: keep producing hard efforts. The ISSN position stand places the clearest evidence in high-intensity efforts lasting roughly 30 seconds to 12 minutes. At elite margins, a small benefit can matter. That does not mean every elite uses it.

The running results are mixed. A review of 11 continuous-running trials found negligible average benefit after adjustments. A newer trial in 21 recreational female runners reported a roughly 32-second average 10K improvement under its specific meal-and-supplement protocol.

Your stomach gets a vote. In a 15-runner trial, bicarbonate capsules caused more gut symptoms than placebo. The hydrogel condition did not—but neither bicarbonate version improved the 800 m time trial after intervals.

Copying an elite protocol is not a race plan. Match the evidence to your event and your tolerance. If considering it, work with a qualified sports dietitian or clinician; the sodium load and gut effects matter. Race morning is a bad first experiment.
